name: Crus cerebri (cerebral peduncle)
summary: The paired ventral pillars of the midbrain, made entirely of descending fibers: corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers occupy the middle three-fifths, flanked by frontopontine fibers medially and parieto-temporo-occipitopontine fibers laterally. The oculomotor nerve emerges from the medial edge into the interpeduncular fossa, and the uncus of the temporal lobe lies against the lateral edge, so a crus lesion produces the Weber syndrome and a herniating uncus produces contralateral hemiparesis or, when it pushes the opposite crus against the tentorium, a falsely localizing ipsilateral hemiparesis (Kernohan notch).

anatomy.location: Ventral midbrain on each side of the interpeduncular fossa, separated from the tegmentum by the substantia nigra, continuous below with the basis pontis and above with the posterior limb of the internal capsule.

subdivisions.name: Middle three-fifths
subdivisions.note: corticobulbar (medial) and corticospinal (lateral) fibers, arm medial to leg

function: Conducts all corticofugal motor traffic from the internal capsule to the pons and spinal cord.

bestView.label: crura as the two anterior bulges of the midbrain flanking the interpeduncular fossa
crus continuing up into the internal capsule

imaging.normalAppearance: The crura are dark compact white matter on T2 forming the anterior contour of the midbrain; the substantia nigra behind them is darker still on T2*. Wallerian degeneration after a hemispheric stroke thins and brightens the ipsilateral crus.

pathology.finding: Paramedian restricted diffusion in the medial crus including the emerging oculomotor fibers.

Medial temporal lobe displaced over the tentorial edge compressing the ipsilateral crus and pushing the midbrain so the contralateral crus is notched by the tentorium; T2 signal in the compressed peduncle.
Atrophy and T2 hyperintensity of the crus months after a large MCA infarct.
pathology.timing: From about 4–10 weeks after the stroke

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI and T2 through the midbrain

lesionEffects.deficit: Contralateral hemiparesis including the lower face and tongue
lesionEffects.mechanism: Corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers in the middle of the crus

lesionEffects.deficit: Ipsilateral third nerve palsy with the hemiparesis (Weber)
lesionEffects.mechanism: Oculomotor fascicle exiting through the medial crus
Contralateral crus compressed against the tentorial edge (Kernohan notch, false localizing)

examination: Limb power, facial and tongue movement on the side opposite the lesion
In a comatose patient with a dilated pupil, remember the hemiparesis may be on the same side as the pupil
pearls: Third nerve palsy plus contralateral hemiparesis is the crus (Weber)
A dilated pupil with ipsilateral hemiparesis means the herniation is on the side of the pupil, not the weakness
